passages.title: Lalu Muhammad Zohri: Indonesia's Sprinting Star
passages.text:
Lalu Muhammad Zohri is an Indonesian sprinter known for competing in short-distance races. He comes from West Nusa Tenggara, and his journey in athletics has drawn attention to the effort needed to develop as a young athlete. Sprinting may look simple because a race lasts only a short time, but preparation involves much more than running fast for a few seconds.

A sprinter trains to improve the start, acceleration, running form, and ability to maintain speed. Coaches may study how an athlete leaves the starting blocks and how each step is placed. Small changes can matter because the race is decided by fractions of a second. Training also includes rest and careful attention to equipment and technique.

Zohri gained international attention after winning the men's 100-metre title at the 2018 World U20 Championships. The result was a notable achievement for Indonesia and showed how a young athlete could compete successfully on an international stage. However, one victory does not mean that training becomes easy or that future results are guaranteed.

His story can encourage students to set goals and work consistently. It also reminds readers that sporting success usually depends on coaching, practice, discipline, and opportunities to compete—not only natural talent.

passages.title: Way Kambas National Park and Elephant Conservation
passages.text:
Way Kambas National Park is in Lampung, on the island of Sumatra. The park is known for its lowland forest, wetlands, and wildlife. It is also associated with efforts to protect Sumatran elephants, whose natural habitat has been affected by human activity and changes in land use.

An elephant is a large animal with complex social behaviour. In conservation work, staff need to understand the animals' needs as well as the environment around them. Monitoring, habitat protection, and public education can all be part of a wider conservation effort. These tasks require time, trained workers, and cooperation among different groups.

The park is not simply a place where visitors look at animals. Protected areas need rules so that human activity does not disturb wildlife. Visitors should follow instructions, keep a safe distance, and avoid feeding or provoking animals. Respectful behaviour helps reduce risks to both people and wildlife.

Conservation also depends on communities living near protected areas. When local people have ways to share concerns and take part in practical solutions, protection efforts can become more realistic. A national park can provide important habitat, but long-term conservation requires continued care, responsible visitors, and cooperation beyond the park boundary.

passages.title: My First Week as a Sports Club Volunteer
passages.text:
Last month, I volunteered at my school's after-class sports club for the first time. I expected to help students practise, but the teacher explained that my main job was to prepare equipment, record attendance, and make sure each group used the correct area.

On Monday, I arrived early and placed cones beside the running track. I forgot to count the cones before the session, so one group had to wait while I looked for the missing ones. The teacher did not shout at me. Instead, she showed me a simple equipment checklist and asked me to use it before every session.

By Wednesday, I was more organised. I checked the list, filled the water container, and wrote down the names of students who arrived late. When two groups wanted the same space, I asked the teacher to confirm the schedule rather than deciding on my own. The session started only a few minutes late.

At the end of the week, the teacher said that I had become more reliable. I learned that volunteering is not only about enjoying sports. It also involves communication, careful preparation, and accepting feedback. Next time, I want to help plan one activity instead of only preparing equipment.

passages.title: How Our Class Reduced Plastic Waste for a Week
passages.text:
Last term, our English teacher asked us to try reducing plastic waste for one school week. We did not have to stop using every plastic item. Instead, we chose a few simple actions that our class could manage.

On Monday, we brought reusable water bottles and counted how many students remembered them. On Tuesday, some students brought lunch in reusable containers. A few forgot, so we reminded each other without making anyone feel embarrassed. On Wednesday, we put a box near the classroom door for clean paper that could be used again for notes.

The hardest day was Thursday because a class activity included packaged snacks. We could not change everything at short notice, but we collected the clean wrappers separately and discussed what we could do differently next time. On Friday, we reviewed the week and shared the ideas that had been easiest to follow.

Our teacher did not announce a dramatic result or claim that we had solved the school's waste problem. We simply noticed that planning ahead made some habits easier. I learned that a small class project works best when the steps are realistic and everyone understands the purpose.

passages.title: The Legend of Sangkuriang
passages.text:
In a well-known version of the Sundanese legend, Dayang Sumbi lived with her son, Sangkuriang. One day, Sangkuriang went hunting with a dog named Tumang. After an argument about the hunt, he returned home angry, and a terrible conflict followed. Dayang Sumbi later sent him away, and he grew up far from her.

Years passed before Sangkuriang returned to the area. He met Dayang Sumbi but did not recognise her as his mother. They became close, and he wanted to marry her. When Dayang Sumbi realised who he was, she was frightened by the situation and tried to stop the marriage without telling him the truth immediately.

She asked Sangkuriang to build a large boat and a lake in a single night. He worked with extraordinary speed, and Dayang Sumbi feared he would finish before morning. She asked people to spread cloth and create the appearance of dawn. Seeing the light, Sangkuriang believed that he had failed to complete the task in time.

Furious, he kicked the unfinished boat away. In the legend, the overturned boat became associated with the shape of Mount Tangkuban Perahu. The story is a traditional explanation connected with a landscape, not a scientific account of how the mountain formed. Versions of the legend may differ in their details.
hints: the boat and Mount Tangkuban Perahu

passages.title: Bawang Merah and Bawang Putih
passages.text:
In a familiar version of the Indonesian folktale, Bawang Putih lived with her stepmother and stepsister, Bawang Merah. Bawang Putih was expected to do most of the household work, while Bawang Merah was treated more kindly. Although she was often tired, Bawang Putih tried to remain patient and helpful.

One day, while washing clothes by a river, Bawang Putih lost a piece of clothing in the water. She searched for it but could not find it. An older woman had found the item and offered to return it, but first asked Bawang Putih to help with some work. Bawang Putih agreed and completed the tasks carefully.

The woman rewarded her and sent her home with a gift. When Bawang Putih returned, her stepmother and Bawang Merah wanted the same reward. Bawang Merah copied the journey, but she was impatient and unwilling to help. In this version, her behaviour led to an unpleasant result rather than the reward she expected.

The contrast between the two sisters is central to the story: Bawang Putih acts with patience, while Bawang Merah expects a reward without showing the same care. The tale is told in different forms, so particular objects and events may change between retellings. Readers should recognise it as folklore rather than a record of a real event.

passages.title: How to Prepare a Balanced Lunchbox
passages.text:
Preparing a balanced lunchbox does not have to be difficult. A useful lunch can include a main food, fruit or vegetables, a protein food, and a drink. Choose familiar foods that are practical for your family to prepare.

First, choose a main food that gives you energy, such as rice, bread, potatoes, or noodles. Pick an amount that suits your appetite and the length of your school day. Next, add fruit and vegetables in different colours when possible. For example, you could pack a banana and cucumber slices, or an orange with carrots.

Then, include a protein food such as eggs, tofu, tempeh, beans, fish, or chicken. You do not need to use an expensive ingredient; choose an option that is available and suitable for you. Bring safe drinking water in a clean, reusable bottle. A refillable bottle can also reduce the need for single-use drink containers.

Food safety is important. Wash your hands before preparing food, use clean containers, and close them properly. Foods that spoil easily should be kept cool when needed. Before leaving home, check that you have your lunchbox, drink, and any spoon or fork you need. A good lunchbox can be simple, familiar, and easy to pack.

passages.title: How to Prepare for a Short Job Interview
passages.text:
A short job interview can feel stressful, but preparation helps you explain your skills clearly. You do not need to memorise a long speech. Instead, learn about the role and prepare a few examples that show what you can do.

First, read the job description carefully. Identify the main tasks and the skills the employer wants. If the description is unclear, write down questions you may ask during the interview. Next, prepare a brief introduction that includes your current situation, relevant experience, and interest in the role.

Then, think of two or three examples from school, volunteering, or previous work. Choose examples that show responsibility, teamwork, problem-solving, or communication. Practise explaining each example in a few sentences: describe the situation, what you did, and the result. Be honest about what you have and have not done.

Before the interview, check the time, location, transport plan, and any documents you need. Choose clean, appropriate clothing and arrive a little early. During the interview, listen to each question before answering. If you do not understand a question, politely ask the interviewer to repeat or explain it. Afterward, note what went well and what you want to improve next time.

passages.title: Should Schools Offer More Sports Clubs?
passages.text:
Schools should offer a range of sports clubs because students have different interests and abilities. A club can give students a regular chance to practise a skill, work with others, and take part in an activity beyond ordinary lessons. However, adding clubs needs thoughtful planning rather than simply filling every afternoon with more tasks.

First, different clubs can make participation more accessible. Some students enjoy team games, while others prefer running, badminton, dance, or individual fitness activities. A range of choices allows students to find an activity that feels suitable to them. Clubs can also provide a place to practise cooperation, follow rules, and learn how to respond to winning or losing.

There are practical limits. Schools need safe spaces, equipment, staff supervision, and time in the timetable. Some students have transport responsibilities or family duties after school. If every club meets at the same time or requires expensive equipment, many students may be unable to join.

For these reasons, schools should expand sports clubs gradually and ask students what activities they want. Low-cost options, shared equipment, and more than one schedule can help. The goal should not be to make every student join a club, but to provide realistic opportunities for those who want to participate.

passages.title: Why Wildlife Conservation Needs Local Communities
passages.text:
Wildlife conservation is more likely to be practical when local communities are included in planning and decision-making. Protected areas and conservation staff are important, but they cannot address every issue alone. People who live near wildlife habitats often understand local routines, concerns, and changes in the environment.

Community members can share observations about animals, damaged habitats, or activities that may create conflict. This information can help conservation teams decide where to focus attention. Local people may also contribute through education, responsible tourism, habitat restoration, or agreed monitoring activities when suitable training and support are available.

However, asking communities to help is not enough by itself. Conservation plans must listen to local concerns and consider how decisions affect people's daily lives. If rules create unfair costs or people are excluded from discussions, cooperation may become difficult. Clear communication and realistic support can make participation more meaningful.

Wildlife protection therefore needs more than signs and boundaries. It needs scientific knowledge, consistent management, and relationships built on trust. When conservation workers and nearby communities share information and responsibilities, they have a better chance of finding solutions that protect wildlife while recognising local needs.
